Good afternoon, Chair and members of the Committee. Uh, my name is Randy Ali. I'm the executive director of the Arab American Family Support Center, known as AFSC. Um, AFSC serves roughly 20,000 people each year across New York City. Over 70% of our clients were born outside of the

United States, and many come from historically underserved communities. AFSC is a MOIA-established legal support center. We create safe and supportive spaces and are a trusted resource— resource for immigrants in a new city. We work with families who are experiencing language barriers, cultural differences, and mistrust of systems that have historically targeted them. That is why trusted community-based organizations like AFSC and our partners play such a critical role in making sure immigrant New Yorkers have access to Know Your Rights information. Since I started in this position in September, I've witnessed our staff, many of whom are also immigrants, respond to a surge in fear, need for basic assistance, and mental health challenges in the communities we serve. The gro— this growing need comes from from inhumane federal immigration policies, hostile anti-immigrant rhetoric, cuts to public benefit, rising food and housing insecurity, and a spike in anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant hate. Our communities are increasingly being targeted. We see this in incidents like the recent attack on young Muslim women in Bay Ridge. Fear in our

communities is profound. Mixed-status families are increasingly choosing to self-deport rather than risk detention or separation by ICE, tearing families apart, even those in the middle of a family reunification process. We have seen a sharp decline in community members applying for naturalization. Uh, this year we did not host our annual citizenship celebration, usually a joyous occasion, because so few members of our community took the exam. Some were afraid to take the test and others had their scheduled test paused due to new restrictions. For families traumatized by conflict in their home countries and concerned about growing conflict in the Middle East, seeking legal help can feel like an additional threat to safety. Families also face rising application fees, long wait times, and widespread misinformation. Our community needs to know their rights and to know their city is protecting them. This legislation will empower them to make the right legal decisions to protect their families. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Thank you. Thank you all.

Thank you. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: The next panel will consist of Dave Basnet from NYIC, Rabbi Adam Graubart, Zachary Ahmad, New York Civil Liberties Union, and Noelle Peñez from the New York Lawyers for the Public Interest. Hi, oh my God.

Um, and the members of the Committee for holding this public hearing. My name is Noelle Penas, and I'm the health justice community organizer at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest. At NYLPI, my colleagues and I work to address the human rights crisis in immigration detention and to advocate for healthcare for all New Yorkers regardless of immigration status. We have heard repeatedly from clients who need and are eligible for life-sustaining medical care but are hesitant to seek healthcare for themselves and their family members at local hospitals due to this fear of immigration enforcement, including disclosure of their private information. We have also heard from medical providers about the lack of guidance and support within their institutions as they endeavor to provide necessary

care to their patients, particularly those who are in civil immigration custody. It is difficult for clients to feel safe seeking care when ICE repeatedly enters our public hospitals without warning or public acknowledgement to the community or clear guidelines to medical providers. This mistrust is compounded when the community learns that our public hospital system has longstanding contracts with Palantir, a technology company with an active $30 million federal contract to identify, track, and deport our immigrant neighbors. This is why we support Intro 55 and 261 and other sanctuary policies like the New York City Trust Act. These actions are critical to preserve access to healthcare for all New Yorkers. We express our support for legislation that would empower our most vulnerable community members with access to information about their rights, and we also support the Trust Act, which would prohibit collaboration between the city immigration authorities. This is essential to maintaining trust in our institutions, supporting public health measures, and ensuring the safety of all New Yorkers when seeking care.

We urge the Council to pass these critical policies, and we also further suggest passing bills that would mandate hospitals to enact safeguards for patients in ICE custody and their medical providers. Given the rising disappearances from ICE, it is now more important than ever to rebuild the bridges of trust between immigrant communities and city government. Thank you again for your support of our work and our clients, and we look forward to continued partnership protecting our communities and their health.

Hello, I'm Rabbi Adam Graubart. Today I'm speaking on behalf of myself and not as a representative of a synagogue. I'm also a proud member of Jews for Racial and Economic Justice. The federal Administration's treatment of immigrants constitutes a moral crisis, and I reject our city government playing any role in the violence happening to our immigrant neighbors. I appreciate the existing restrictions against collaboration with ICE, but the City Council must swiftly pass the TRUST Act to ensure that we are protecting immigrant New Yorkers in our fullest capacity. We've seen numerous violations of our

current laws, and immigrants have taken the hit. Jewish tradition teaches about accountability. In fact, Jewish communities dedicate an entire season each year towards Cheshbon HaNefesh, accounting of the soul, in which every person evaluates their past actions against what is kind and just. In Leviticus, the Israelites receive the charge, tochiach et amitecha, reprove your fellow when they have done wrong. These particular principles shape my view of how to achieve universal justice. When harm occurs, each of us can name it and work to address it. In this way, the individual may learn and grow while the society avoids repeating the negative consequences of the behavior. When government workers endanger immigrants, we need to empower individual New Yorkers to call out violations of the law and prevent perpetual harm. That's why we must pass the TRUST Act now. Jewish texts and history also teach me that everyone is better off when we embrace the migrants in our midst and what they have to offer our society. Therefore, in adv— in addition to advancing the TRUST Act, I ask the City Council to close loopholes in existing sanctuary protections by passing

Introduction 55 and Int— Introduction 261 as soon as possible. Thank you.

Good morning. My name is Zach Ahmad. I'm a senior policy counsel at the New York Civil Liberties Union, and we are a member of the ICE Out NYC Coalition. The NYCLU has long been a defender of and an advocate for strengthening our city's sanctuary laws. New York City's laws and policies keeping the city out of the business of immigration enforcement are a proud distinction for our city, which has always been a magnet for immigrants from across the world. Our city is in a moment of hopeful transition as we move from a Mayoral Administration that actively sought to undermine our sanctuary laws to a new Administration that has already begun to take tangible steps towards ensuring these laws are properly implemented through the issuance of Executive Order 13 and the establishment of the Interagency Response Committee. It is welcoming and encouraging that this Committee, under new leadership, chose to begin its work by examining the state of our sanctuary city

protections and considering legislation to bolster them. We are grateful for the council's continued oversight to ensure that New York City is keeping its promises to the millions of immigrants who call the city home. Hopeful as this moment is, It is— as the Committee undertakes that task, it must be clear-eyed about the many instances that advocates and the city's own Department of Investigation have uncovered where sanctuary laws were clearly violated. Some of those examples were discussed at length in a separate Committee hearing just days ago, and it is safe to assume that there are many other examples over the years that simply never came to light. The Committee must also not overlook the significant gaps in the way that our loopholes and vaguely worded exceptions undercut the effectiveness of sanctuary laws. As meaningful as New York City sanctuary protections have been over several decades, they remain beset by exceptions that allow for collusion with ICE based on a person's past criminal legal system contact, and that permit opaque task force arrangements to continue to keep— that continue to

keep local officers in contact with federal immigration enforcement. Two bills on today's agenda, Intro 55, er, and Intro 261, uh, are a positive step in that direction, but we still need more. The Council must prioritize passing the New York City Trust Act, Intro 209, and create a mechanism to hold key city agencies accountable that violate our laws for misconduct and incentivize them to take those laws seriously. The Council must also revisit legislation to remove the confusing and crim— and, and the confusing and misguided criminal carve-outs that exist in our city's detainer laws which not only impose double punishment on people who satisfied their sentences, but also invite mistakes that then unlawfully punish people— funnel people into ICE custody. Thank you

Good afternoon, Chair Encarnación and members of the Committee. Uh, thank you for the opportunity to testify today on the key legislation, uh, and critical steps that this body has to take to make sure that New Yorkers are both aware of their rights and ensure that mechanisms for accounting accountability are created for New Yorkers if city agencies violate their rights.

My name is Dave Basnet, and I'm the senior immigrant— immigration rights policy manager at the New York Immigration Coalition, a coalition of more than 200 immigrant and refugee organizations advancing access to public services, inclusion, and justice. Today's hearing and proposed legislation recognizes that laws alone are not enough and that New Yorkers must know their rights in order for those protections to have any real meaning. New York City has reliably been a national leader in upholding our municipal protections for immigrant communities through our longstanding sanctuary laws, fought for by this very same body. But those protections only work when New Yorkers, uh, city workers, and institutions clearly understand them. At a time when fear and confusion about federal enforcement increases, New York's NYIC hopes that this hearing leads the Council to take necessary steps to strengthen transparency, rebuild trust between immigrant communities and city government, and ensure that accurate information about legal rights and city policies is consistently accessible across our public institutions.

By focusing on education and visibility, the Council can help ensure that those protections that are already written into city law are fully realized. Today, NYIC, alongside the ICE Out NYC coalition, is testifying on behalf of Intro 55, the New York City Know Your Rights Act, and calls for the swift passage and action by this body on Intro 209, the New York City Trust Act. We offer our strong support for Intro 55, uh, this bill would require the Commissioner of MOIA in consultation with the city's law department to develop signage that identifies in non-public areas of city property and outlines the rights individuals may invoke when interacting with federal authorities. In NYIC, the- steers the Education Collaborative, which is a coalition of more than 30 grassroots organizations and practitioners working to improve these things. And from an education perspective, Intro 55 would strengthen trust with school communities by ensuring that all students, families, and staff clearly know their rights. Uh, we look forward to the Council acting on the New York City Trust Act and the New York City Know Your Rights Act. Thank you so much.

CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Thank you, thank you all. Our next panel, I'm calling up Shelley English, Jasmine Lately, um, just— hmm, oh, Sandhu too? I'm so sorry, I thought that was an L. It's this— it's the handwriting. Uh, Dr. Betty from Health Justice for NY and Dr. Steve from— also from Health Justice, uh, and— oh, there you go. Thank you. When you're ready, you may begin.

Hi, my name is Shelley English. I'm here with other members of Health Justice for New York in support of Intros 55 and 261 with amendments. I'm the daughter of an immigrant. I'm a former city— New York City employee, and I currently serve as a New York State licensed mental health counselor. A doctor in France and a doctor in Italy in the early 1940s prevented the Gestapo from arresting and deporting my grandmother and mother to their deaths. Because of these doctors, I'm here today helping neighbors and patients I care for and care about in the city I call home. I'm honored to be surrounded by today's healers and to speak on behalf of Health Justice for New York. Immigrants and refugees in New York City and our nation are vital and irrepre— replaceable part of our

history, our communities, and our economy. Immigrants create economic opportunity for those of us born within and outside the United States. Immigrants pay more in taxes than received in services, including healthcare. Immigrants are essential workers from building construction to food delivery to childcare, and immigrants are a cornerstone of healthcare workers, including doctors, nurses, hospital aides, homecare attendants, and facility maintenance workers. Under the guise of immigration enforcement, more and more people are being lawlessly snatched off the streets by anonymous armed bullies in masks and brought injury to our emergency departments. Our family, friends, colleagues, and neighbors are increasingly fearful as patients or workers traveling to or spending time at healthcare facilities. As a trauma specialist who conducts psychological evaluations of immigrants seeking asylum, I'm an eyewitness to the fear and anxiety of patients afraid that ICE agents might show up at any time, anywhere to handcuff them and take them away to deportation centers.

We urge that federal immigration enforcement agents and agencies stay out of all healthcare facilities except for limited access in narrow circumstances with verified legal documents. All patients and healthcare workers deserve privacy and safety in healthcare, including physical and mental safety and data protections. When federal immigration agents are present in healthcare facilities, they interfere with the privacy, safety, and care for all patients and staff.

Good afternoon, my name is Dr. Jasmeet Sandhu, member of Health Justice for NY Doctors Council Union. For Intro 55, we believe signage is important. Public healthcare facilities should be explicitly included, and existing worker tenant rights signage should be expanded so that the information is widely distributed in public and private settings. Our members work in healthcare facilities across the city, including public hospitals that have had federal immigration agents on premises. These events, including detained people brought in by agents who injured them, have sown fear among patients and staff because we still lack clear policies and procedures

in our facilities and the signage and information to communicate these policies and procedures. We support Intro 55, including across all public healthcare facilities; this is including H&H. At Elmhurst Hospital, the facility that I work at, our facility is proud of our diverse staff, many who are immigrants. Elmhurst is also an academic hospital whose trainees include medical students on visas. Members are asking me what require— what areas require a warrant for an agent to enter? What is a valid warrant? It is vital for our— to make sure our staff and patients know what areas are public versus private, protecting our sick patients and their privacy. Members have also voiced clear signage would avoid confusion and prepare staff to follow the appropriate protocol for that designated area. The presence of ICE agents in our facilities does impact the care we can provide. Patients are delaying care, ending up in critical conditions because they are worried that they'll encounter an agent. Family members are too afraid to visit their sick loved ones for the same reason.

Health Justice for NY has developed comprehensive guidelines for healthcare facilities. We urge the Committee to review them. We also believe companion legislation is necessary to create more specific policies and procedures that are reflected in signage. Thank you.

Good afternoon. I'm Dr. Betty Kolod, a primary care physician in East Harlem and a member of Health Justice for New York, also Chair of the Board of Physicians for our national health program, New York Metro. I'm speaking in support of Intro 261. To protect the safety and privacy of patients and staff in healthcare facilities, the city must cancel and never initiate contracts with immigration enforcement entities. I'm particularly troubled that New York City Health and Hospitals contracts with Palantir, known to be heavily involved in federal immigration enforcement. My patient Carmen has liver cancer. Her devoted son is a mama's boy and takes her to chemotherapy and palliative care visits for the searing pain in her stomach. She has lived in Harlem for 35 years, so he was shocked to discover that Carmen does not have

legal status. I was unaware too, because all low-income persons over the age of 65 in New York are eligible of Medicaid— eligible for Medicaid regardless of their immigration status. Now that this understanding has emerged, Carmen has been missing appointments and has decided not to pursue a cure for her cancer. She cannot risk having her protect— protected health information, including immigration status, unlawfully shared with federal, federal agencies directly or via private entities, and has decided to die at home with dignity instead. Intro 261 would protect Carmen and it could be made stronger. Public healthcare facilities like H&H and its Gotham affiliates should be named explicitly. The bill language should also be explicit that the city shall not procure goods or services from contracted entities engaged in immigration enforcement. Language should be added that existing contracts will be canceled if in violation of the Intro, and that all existing contracts will be reviewed prior to renewal. Additional legislation should require public healthcare institutions to create clear policies and

procedures for interactions with federal immigration agents. As Health Justice for New York, we will provide our policy recommendations in writing. Thank you for protecting us and our patients.

My name is Dr. Steve Auerbach. I am also a member of Health Justice for New York. I'm a retired US Public Health Service officer with Federal Health and Human Services and also on the board of B&HP New York. We're healthcare workers speaking for over 1,000 members of Health Justice for New York in support of Intros 55-261, though we do have some, uh, urged amendments. Health Justice for New York grew out of multiple organizations, including New York Doctors Coalition, founded in 2016 after that year's election. We're an informal collective of health workers and advocates providing expertise drawn from our lived experience and solidarity with social justice movements and our patients. We would urge that Intro 55, uh, have some additional language explicitly naming, perhaps in Section C, explicitly naming Health Hospitals and its Gotham affiliates. Uh, we

would also ask that Intro 55 or other, uh, city, uh, legislation go further to include the private healthcare facilities, the so-called, uh, private voluntary hospitals and the clinics and the FQHCs and the rest to protect health workers, what, and help patients regardless of whether they are public or private. Um, we, uh, urge this Committee along with others, um, appropriate City Council Committees, uh, such as Committee on Hospitals, the Mayoral offices and agencies working on immigration to continue actively engaging health workers and advocates. We are here today because management at Health AND Hospitals and management at the private hospitals have refused, uh, to, uh, protect their pa— uh, patients and their providers. They refuse to engage with, uh, activist employees who, um, are aligned with the goals of this Committee. Um, and we are asking that, uh, the city government, uh, at all levels engage with hospital management, both public and private, uh, to make sure that the sanctuary, uh, laws are actually applied. Thank you.

CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: And, um, the policies that you have, you have copies for— to leave with us? Okay, perfect. Thank you so much. Uh, we're now calling up Charles Brown from Lutheran Social Services of New York. Guvir Singh Sidhu. Yes, please. Thank you and Rabbi Marisa James. Oh, sorry and Brennan Peacore-Brink from the Interfaith Center of New York. Hello. Once you're ready, you can begin.

Good afternoon, and thank you to the Committee on Immigration for the opportunity to testify. My name is Brennan Peacore-Brink, and I serve as the director for migrant outreach at the Interfaith Center of New York. Founded in 1997, the mission of the Interfaith Center is to overcome prejudice, violence, and misunderstanding by activating the power of New York's grassroots religious and civic leaders and their communities. I want to attempt to tell two brief stories that illustrate the need for Intro 55 and Sound Know Your Rights trainings. An Imam in our network called me. A congregant had just rushed into the mosque and headed straight

to the restroom, uh, because he was sick to his stomach. The imam wasn't calling me over a simple stomach bug or food poisoning. No, the Imam conveyed to me that the congregant had a sharp, urgent pain, like his stomach was splitting in two. I said, Imam, I think you need to take the individual to an H&H hospital. There will be low or no cost. I know, the Imam replied to me, but you don't understand, Brennan. He's too scared. He's scared ICE will be there or that the hospital will let ICE get him. While I could point to New York's sanctuary laws, I couldn't point to visible signs that the hospital had actually been trained on their rights and would exert them. So we didn't go to the hospital. The second story: grassroots organizations now working with Hands Off New York have distributed Know Your Rights materials to over 7,000 NYC businesses. In my neighborhood, parents want to take the same model to distribute Know Your Rights signs and information to their schools. However, their schools aren't sure if they can accept and display these signs. They need guidance— simple, obvious guidance that affirms that our schools can tell every student

they will be safe and that the school will work to keep them safe. In both of these stories, clarity and leadership from the city in the form of Intro 55 would support New Yorkers. It would give those sick the assurance that they can seek the care they need, a key public health support not only for immigrant New Yorkers but all New Yorkers who want— who benefit from healthy neighbors. Intro 55 would do the same in our schools, give students and families more confidence that their schools will properly understand and exert their rights and the rights of students. Again, this strengthens not only our education system for immigrant students but all students. Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Encarnación and members of the Committee on Immigration. My name is Gurvir Singh Sidhu. I serve as a state policy manager at the Sikh Coalition, uh, the nation's largest Sikh civil rights organization. I'm also here as the son of immigrants. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today in support of Intro 55 and 261. The Sikh Coalition was

founded in the aftermath of September 11th, 2001. To defend the civil rights of Sikh Americans and to ensure that people of all faiths and backgrounds can live free from discrimination and fear. Today, many Sikh New Yorkers, including asylum seekers, immigrants, and mixed-status families, are directly affected by immigration enforcement policies and the growing confusion about their legal rights in interactions with immigration authorities. Indro 55 addresses this gap by helping ensure that immigrant New Yorkers clearly understand their constitutional rights. When federal immigration authorities appear in or near city facilities, many individuals don't know what protections apply, what city policies allow, or how to assert their rights. Clear multilingual signage explaining these protections and identifying the boundaries between public and non-public spaces helps ensure that residents, families, and city employees understand the law and can act accordingly. We hope to see continued expansion of materials available in various languages spoken by our

immigrant communities. Intro 261 is equally important. New York City resources shouldn't be used in ways that undermine trust between immigrant communities and local government. When immigrant New Yorkers fear that accessing local services could expose them to immigration enforcement, they're less likely to seek healthcare, send their children to school, report crimes, or access city programs. Sikhs who have experienced hate crimes or whose children experience severe school bullying should have the confidence in the respective institutions not to endanger them further. This erosion of trust harms families, weakens community stability, and ultimately undermines public safety. These issues carry particular significance for Sikh communities. Many Sikhs are visible— ident— visibly identifiable because of our articles of faith. Um, thank you for uh, your leadership and the time to speak here today. We hope you pass this legislation to protect the civil rights of individuals.

Uh, good afternoon. Thank you, Chair Encarnación, and to the Committee and staff for

holding today's hearing. My name is Charles Brown. I'm the director of the Immigration Legal Program at Lutheran Social Services of New York, and I'm here to testify in support of Intro 55. The Immigration Legal Program at Lutheran has provided high-quality legal services to New Yorkers for over 25 years. We have a focus in humanitarian relief, including assisting New Yorkers seeking asylum and special immigrant juvenile status. In our experience, federal immigration law is complicated and confusing. When you add the intersection of local, state, and federal laws, it can be nearly impossible to understand when it is legal or what is legal when it comes to immigration enforcement. Confusion about the law is then a breeding ground for disinformation and misinformation. As a result, community members, immigrants, and otherwise often lack accurate, clear, and current information about the state of the law. This misinformation can both create fear and can embolden questionable and illegal immigration enforcement tactics.

This bill aims to remedy that information gap by providing clear signage in multiple languages and age-appropriate throughout the city, informing the community about key rights around immigration and enforcement, city property, and city resources. Community visiting buildings with the signage and those working in the same building stand to benefit from clear information. The signage will also help ensure that New Yorkers understand the law, the first step in empowering them to assert their rights. For these reasons, Lutheran Social Services of New York supports this bill and its aim. Meanwhile, we urge the City Council to provide sustained investment in organizations on the ground serving our immigrant families, friends, and neighbors, such as through the Aslan and, and Pro Se Plus initiatives and through the ICare Coalition, where legal service organizations such as Lutheran are expanding access to legal representation throughout the city. Thank you for your time.

Good afternoon. Uh, my name is Marisa James. I am one of the Rabbis at Congregation Beit Simchat Torah, CBST. Where our ARC immigration

clinic is one of the largest pro se clinics in New York City and we are the conveners of the New York City Pro Se Collaborative. I wanna offer gratitude to the City Council for their consistent support. It's very good to be testifying to partners in this work rather than adversaries. We are an LGBTQ Jewish community with members who are immigrants and the descendants of immigrants, and the majority of the immigrant friends our clinic serves are LGBTQ+ and/or HIV positive. Because of who we serve, we hear stories every day from some of the most vulnerable immigrants in this city. As asylum seekers from countries where LGBTQ+ people are discriminated against or attacked, they can experience the same bigotry here that they faced at home and don't always trust organizations that support people from their country of origin or ethnicity. Many cannot even tell their community or their family the reason why they are seeking asylum here. They come here because of our protections of their rights. But if you don't know your rights, then you don't have access to your rights. Signs in simple,

clear language that explain and reinforce the rights and protections immigrants have in New York City are important in as many languages as possible, in as many places as possible. Our staff often reassure immigrant New Yorkers that city government workers are mostly restricted from collaborating with immigration enforcement, but some of them are skeptical and as a result forgo benefits that all New Yorkers, regardless of immigration status, are eligible to receive. The clear official signage in every possible kind of city building would go a long way to help convince some immigrant New Yorkers much more than our reassurances. On top of this, many in our community are afraid to even leave home given the current immigration enforcement context and how they see this in the media. Signage in shelters, schools, and other New York City buildings that people pass through every day could make a real impact in reducing these fears. Um, and just to say, my great-grandparents came to New York City and did not face this kind of a massive bureaucracy in a language they did not know. They never really became fluent in English, and yet they

were New Yorkers who raised 3 more generations of New Yorkers. Um, so I hope that what we can do and what you can do can help reduce that wall, or at least help people pass that wall so that this generation of immigrants can raise the next 4 generations of New Yorkers. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Thank you. Um, I will now call up, uh, Samantha Sanchez from Common Cause, Tanya Matos from Unlocal, Barbara Lopez also from Unlocal, Funmi— Funmi Akinnawonu. Ake— sere? Say it again? Akinnawonu. Oh, I like that. Yep, you had it the first time. There you go.

Sorry. Good afternoon, Chair Encarnación and members of the Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Samantha Sanchez, and I'm the policy manager with Common Cause New York. Common Cause is a nonpartisan watchdog organization dedicated to strengthening democracy, protecting constitutional rights, and ensuring government accountability. We appreciate the Council for holding this, this oversight hearing today and considering Introductions

55 and 261 at a time when immigrant communities in New York City are facing heightened fear and uncertainty due to increased federal immigration enforcement activities. New York City's sanctuary laws exist for a fundamental reason: local government should serve its residents, not function as an extension of federal immigration enforcement. When residents fear that accessing services, entering government buildings, and interacting with city agencies could expose them to immigration enforcement, trust and government deteriorates. That erosion of trust discourages people from seeking services, reporting crimes, or engaging with public institutions, ultimately undermining public safety and effective governance. Intro 55 is an important measure for transparency and accountability. By requiring signage explaining constitutional protections, this legislation helps clarify the legi— the legal boundaries of governing access to city facilities. Intro 261 addresses another important gap. A city that has committed itself to sanctuary protections

should not use taxpayer dollars to contract with entities engaged in immigration enforcement activities. Public procurement decisions should align with the city's legal commitments and policies. Aligning contracting practices with sanctuary policy strengthens the credibility of these protections and ensures that public funds aren't used in ways that undermine the city's own laws. Legislation alone won't solve these challenges, unfortunately. Effective sanctuary protections require clear agency protocols, proper training for city employees, and strong oversight for compliance. New York City has long been a leader in protecting immigrant communities, but real leadership goes beyond laws. It demands implementation. Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

Good afternoon, Chair Encarnación, members of the, um, Immigration Committee. My name is Funmi Akinnawonu. I'm a senior policy analyst at the Federation of Protestant Welfare Agencies. We are an organization that advocates for economic security for New Yorkers, and we have a membership base of over 170 organizations who are

human services agencies and members of faith-based institutions. And so we are here today to support Intro 55 because having prominently displayed signage that informs New Yorkers of their rights is essential to protecting all individual rights of New Yorkers across New York City, and particularly immigrant communities. Um, and we are heartened to hear earlier today the Commissioner talk about all of the public information campaigns that do exist through MOIA. And, um, but we are urging the city to make sure that we are educating immigrant communities both about their rights and protections as well as their privileges within, um, ah, through New York City government. And so we are advocating for an increase in funding for immigration legal services as well as increasing Know Your Rights campaigns and for our human services agencies. Our members of both the faith-based institutions and the human services agencies are where people find community, practice their faiths, and receive direct services. And the changes in immigration policy as well as funding, uh, for example, for, um, both the removal and then the

restoration of funding for organizations like entities like AmeriCorps, which are instrumental to building up our human services sector, have had a huge impact on those agencies and their ability to provide direct services, uh, as well as, um, the constant fear within those organizations and the anxiety around having to address what they would do, um, if CBP or ICE showed up at their doors. Um, we are also advocating for increased public education, particularly around changes to public charge, which could have a chilling effect for immigrants when it comes to, um, utilizing public benefits and for increased funding to CCHR in order to operationalize a lot of public information campaigns through the city. Thank you very much.

Good afternoon, Chair, uh, Encarnación, um, and members of the Immigration Committee. My name is Tania Mattos and I'm the executive director of Unlocal, uh, a nonprofit organization dedicated to serving New York's immigrant communities through immigration legal services and community education. Our team of lawyers, advocates, organizers, and social workers provide free services to, to immigrant

communities across the 5 boroughs, including Know Your Rights workshops, New York State Dream Act application support, legal representation, social work services, and community events. Through our work in the Pro Se Plus project and the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative and our anti-detention approach that focuses on legal representation, equipping immigrant communities with the tools and emergency preparedness resources that, that need to respond safely and effectively in the event of federal immigration enforcement. Today I'm here to express my strong support for Intro 55 and Intro 261. Through our work, uh, uh, through the Dreamer Center, uh, we are distributing Know Your Rights information and deportation defense materials. We have seen firsthand the value of our city's sanctuary protections and the resources available for immigrant communities. But these protections only work if people know they exist and all agencies follow the law. In recent months, we have heard increasing concern from community members about the presence of ICE in their neighborhoods and uncertainty about the role of the NYPD Police Department. Our communities

deserve clear, visible information about their rights. Access to this information should be treated as a right, not a privilege and Intro 55 ensures that people are informed of their protection in a clear and prominent way. It helps prevent the risk of unlawful collaboration between local agencies and federal immigration enforcement. I also strongly support Intro 261, which would prohibit New York City from contracting with entities engaged in immigration enforcement. The current deportation agenda is tearing families apart, and I, I thank you for introducing these bills. Uh, thank you for the opportunity to testify. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay, the next, uh, person will have interpretation services, so there'll be 2 minutes and then 2 minutes added for the, uh, interpretation as well.

[SPEAKING IN SPANISH 149:43-151:21] Mi comunidad empeora cada día más. Hoy estoy aquí para darle fe de lo que está sucediendo en mi comunidad de Sunset Park. Y lo importante que es que aprueben las medidas necesarias y protección de

los inmigrantes. La actividad de ICE en mi vecindario ha aumentado en los últimos meses.
